Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM)

Following the Score Matching with Langevin Dynamics (SMLD), Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) (Ho, Jain, and Abbeel 2020) formulated a Diffusion Models (DMs) as two separate processes. The forward, or diffusion process was defined as a fixed Markov chain that increasingly adds noise to the original data \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), being described as: \[ q(\boldsymbol{x}_{1:T}\mid \boldsymbol{x}_0) = \prod_{t=1}^T q(\boldsymbol{x}_t\mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}), \tag{1}\] where \(T\in \mathbb N\) is the number of states in the chain. Each transition in this process can be expressed as: \[ q(\boldsymbol{x}_t\mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}) = \mathcal N\left(\boldsymbol{x}_t\mid \sqrt{1-\beta_t}\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}, \beta_t\boldsymbol{I}\right), \tag{2}\] where \(\{\beta_i\}_{i=1}^T\) is a variance schedule. The diffusion process admits sampling any step in the chain directly from the original sample, with the following: \[ \boldsymbol x_t = \sqrt{\overline{\alpha}_t}\boldsymbol x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \overline{\alpha}_t} \boldsymbol \epsilon, \tag{3}\] where \(\alpha_t = 1 - \beta_t\), \(\overline{\alpha}_t = \prod_{s=1}^t \alpha_s\) and \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\mid\boldsymbol{0}, \boldsymbol{I})\).

The reverse process is a Markov chain where the Gaussian transitions are learned via a parametrized Neural Network (NN). Starting \(\boldsymbol{x}_T\sim\mathcal N(\boldsymbol{x}_T\mid \boldsymbol{0}, \boldsymbol{I})\), the NN parametrized by \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) approximates the following chain: \[ p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\left(\boldsymbol{x}_{0:T}\right) = p(\boldsymbol x_T) \prod_{t=1}^T p_{\boldsymbol \theta}(\boldsymbol x_{t-1}\mid \boldsymbol x_t). \tag{4}\] Each transition step is expressed as: \[ p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t}) = \mathcal N\left(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}\mid {\boldsymbol\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t), {\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t)\right). \tag{5}\] That is, the DM learns the mean \({\boldsymbol\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t)\) and variance \({\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t)\) to reverse the noise from \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t}\) to \(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}\). To achieve this, the model is conditioned on the time step \(t\).

The NN is trained to minimize the negative log likelihood of the data. Making some algebraic steps: \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal L(\boldsymbol{\theta}) &= \mathbb E\left[ -\log p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol{x}_0)\right] \leq \mathbb E_q\left[- \log\frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{0:T})}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{1:T} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_0)}\right] \\ &= \mathbb E_q\left[- \log p(\boldsymbol{x}_T) - \sum_{t\geq 1} \log\frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1})}\right] \\ &= \mathbb E_q\left[- \log p(\boldsymbol{x}_T) - \log \frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{0} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_1)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{0})} - \sum_{t> 1}\log \frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1})}\right]. \end{aligned} \tag{6}\] Applying Bayes’ Theorem to the forward Markov chain: \[ \begin{aligned} &= \mathbb E_q\left[- \log p(\boldsymbol{x}_T) - \log \frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{0} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_1)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{0})} - \sum_{t> 1} \log \frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t)q(\boldsymbol x_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_0)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t}, \boldsymbol{x}_0) q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{0})} \right] \\ &= \mathbb E_q\left[- \log \frac{p(\boldsymbol{x}_T)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_T \mid \boldsymbol{x}_0)} - \log p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{0} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_1)- \sum_{t> 1} \log \frac{p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t)}{q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t}, \boldsymbol{x}_0)}\right] \\ &= \mathbb E_q\bigg[ \underbrace{D_{\text{KL}} \bigg(q(\boldsymbol{x}_T \mid \boldsymbol{x}_0) \parallel p(\boldsymbol{x}_T) \bigg)}_{\mathcal L_T} \underbrace{- \log p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (\boldsymbol x_{0} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_1)}_{\mathcal L_0} \\ &\qquad \qquad \qquad + \sum_{t> 1} \underbrace{D_{\text{KL}} \bigg(q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_{t}, \boldsymbol{x}_0) \parallel p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x} _t) \bigg)}_{\mathcal L_{t-1}}\bigg], \end{aligned} \tag{7}\] where \(D_{\text{KL}}\) is the Kullback-Leibler divergence. Note that by fixing the forward process, the term \(\mathcal L_T\) does not depend on \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) and can therefore be ignored. For the \(\mathcal L_{1:T-1}\) terms, the variance of the NN is fixed to \({\boldsymbol\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) = \sigma_t^2\boldsymbol{I} = \beta_t \boldsymbol{I}\).

With the variance fixed, the KL divergence in the \(\mathcal{L}_{t-1}\) terms compares two Gaussian distributions. This simplifies to the mean squared error between their means. The posterior \(q(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t, \boldsymbol{x}_0)\) is also a Gaussian, therefore, minimizing \(\mathcal{L}_{t-1}\) is equivalent to minimizing the difference between the true posterior mean \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_t\) and the NN’s predicted mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\): \[ \mathcal L_{t-1} = \mathbb E_q \left[ \frac{1}{2\sigma_t^2} \left\| \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_t(\boldsymbol{x}_t, \boldsymbol{x}_0) - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) \right\|^2 \right] + C, \tag{8}\] where \(C\) is a constant independent of \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). With some reparametrization tricks, it is possible to show that these terms can be expressed as: \[ \mathcal L_{t-1} = \mathbb E_{\boldsymbol{x}_0, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}} \left[ \frac{\beta_t^2}{2\sigma_t^2 \alpha_t (1 - \overline{\alpha}_t)} \left\| \boldsymbol{\epsilon} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) \right\|^2 \right], \tag{9}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t)\) is the noise predicted by the NN. It was observed that ignoring the weighting term lead to better results. This results in the final simplified objective function used to train DDPMs: \[ \mathcal L(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbb E_{t, \boldsymbol{x}_0, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}} \left[ \left\| \boldsymbol{\epsilon} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) \right\|^2 \right]. \tag{10}\]

After training the NN \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\) to approximate the noise added to the data, the model can be used to generate new samples from the learned data distribution \(p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\). The reverse process begins by sampling pure Gaussian noise \(\boldsymbol{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0}, \boldsymbol{I})\) and iteratively denoising it down to \(t=0\). The iterative process is described by: \[ \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(\boldsymbol{x}_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\overline{\alpha}_t}} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t)\right) + \sigma_t\boldsymbol{z}, \tag{11}\] where \(\boldsymbol{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0}, \boldsymbol{I})\) for \(t > 1\). At the final step when \(t = 1\), \(\boldsymbol{z} = \boldsymbol{0}\) is set to output the deterministic mean, as adding noise at the very end would degrade the final image.

Code

Importing the packages.

import torch
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from torchvision import transforms
from torchvision.datasets import MNIST
from diffusers import DDPMScheduler, UNet2DModel

Plotting the noise schedule of DDPM.

T = 1000
scheduler = DDPMScheduler(num_train_timesteps=T, beta_schedule="linear")

betas = scheduler.betas.numpy()
alphas = scheduler.alphas.numpy()
alphas_cumprod = scheduler.alphas_cumprod.numpy()

steps = np.arange(1, T + 1)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))
axes[0].plot(steps, betas, color="crimson", linewidth=2)
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\beta_t$", fontsize=14)
axes[0].set_xlabel(r"$t$")

axes[1].plot(steps, alphas, color="blue", linewidth=2)
axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\alpha_t$", fontsize=14)
axes[1].set_xlabel(r"$t$")

axes[2].plot(steps, alphas_cumprod, color="purple", linewidth=2)
axes[2].set_ylabel(r"$\bar{\alpha}_t$", fontsize=14)
axes[2].set_xlabel(r"$t$")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Showing the diffusion process.

dataset = MNIST(root="./data", train=True, download=True, transform=transforms.ToTensor())
x0, _ = dataset[0]
x0 = x0.unsqueeze(0) * 2.0 - 1.0

selected_t = [0, 100, 300, 600, 999]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(selected_t), figsize=(16, 3))

epsilon = torch.randn_like(x0)

for i, t in enumerate(selected_t):
    if t == 0:
        xt = x0
        title = r"Original $\mathbf{x}_0$"
    else:
        t_tensor = torch.tensor([t], dtype=torch.long)
        xt = scheduler.add_noise(x0, epsilon, t_tensor)
        title = r"$t=$" + f"{t}"

    img = (xt.squeeze().numpy() + 1.0) / 2.0
    axes[i].imshow(img, cmap="gray")
    axes[i].set_title(title, fontsize=12)
    axes[i].axis("off")

plt.show()
